title: Maddi in the forest
hook: Vessantara's wife comes home with fruit to find her children gone (Jataka 547)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vessantara, read whole: the elephant, the exile, the gifts, the homecoming. Your line was the last life. Did you notice what one of your gifts cost? Today, the scene we left for later. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

A basket of fruit, roots and leaves, heavy on her hip. Maddi has been gathering in the forest all day, the way she does every day, so her children will have something to eat when she gets home. The night before, she slept badly, troubled by a frightening dream, and she told her husband about it. He told her not to worry. Now the light is going, and she is late. Something keeps standing in her path. Today, the Vessantara tale from the mother's side.
screen: `A BASKET OF FRUIT.` → `A BAD DREAM.` → `THE LIGHT IS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the beasts on the path. In the tale, a lion, a tiger and a leopard stand across her road and won't move. The tale tells us what Maddi doesn't know: they're gods in animal shape, holding her back so she can't come home in the middle of the gift. She pleads with them to let her through, and only at nightfall do they step aside. Second, the empty hermitage. Every evening the children run out to meet her. Tonight nobody runs. She calls their names. She looks in the places where they played, by the pond, under the trees. Vessantara, sitting there, at first says nothing. Third, the long night. Maddi searches the whole night through, and at dawn she falls at her husband's feet as if dead. He sprinkles water on her face to bring her round, and only then does he tell her: he has given the children away to a brahmin, so that he might reach awakening. Fourth, her answer. The tale has her rejoice in the gift, and join her merit to his. Some readers find that ending hard to accept. Others hear in it a love that has already been tested by the worst night of her life. The tale does not hurry past her grief. It gives her search room to breathe, line after line, place after place. Tradition says that where the whole tale is recited aloud at festivals, Maddi's search is a part listeners wait for, and weep through. A story told for the sake of generosity stops, for a long time, to stand beside a mother looking for her children in the dark.
screen: `A LION, A TIGER, A LEOPARD.` · `NOBODY RUNS TO MEET HER.` · `SHE SEARCHES ALL NIGHT.` · `SHE REJOICES IN THE GIFT.` · then, large: `MADDI'S GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a parent's love. In Maddi's tale, love looks like worry: a late return, an empty hut, a search that lasts all night. Bring to mind a time someone who cared for you worried about you. A night they waited up, a call that came more than once, a face at the door when you finally got home. At the time it might have looked like fuss. Look at it now as care with nowhere else to go. If that relationship is a painful one, you can choose anyone whose care reached you. If it feels right, silently wish them well, wherever they are. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maddi. The mother who came home with fruit and searched all night for her children. Today's word.
Your line: Maddi's grief. Today, when you hear someone's worry about a person they love, slow down and let them say all of it before you answer. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Where the Vessantara tale is recited aloud, Maddi's chapter may be chanted slowly and with feeling, and audiences listen to it as part of a merit-making festival.

original.note: Pali: Maddi, Vessantara's wife in the last tale of the Jataka.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side character in a story about a generous man.
what it means: the mother whose long night of searching gives the tale its grief.
what a scholar hears: the gods delay her on purpose so the gift can be made; the tale then slows down to follow her search, and that is the part of the recitation listeners are said to weep through.

notes: Confirm details: Maddi's bad dream the night before and Vessantara reassuring her; three gods as lion, tiger and leopard blocking her until nightfall; children's habit of running out to meet her; her night-long search; fainting at dawn; Vessantara reviving her with water; her rejoicing in (approving) the gift.
In some recensions Vessantara first speaks harshly to Maddi (accusing her of dawdling) before telling her; left out as unsure. Keeper may wish to add it.
'Tradition says ... listeners wait for, and weep through' is attributed, not asserted; confirm for Thai/Lao recitation practice (the Matsi chapter of the Thet Mahachat).
Practice allows for listeners with painful parent relationships; confirm tone.

Editor pass: practice reworked around a time someone worried about the listener, because day 840's practice already asked for one ordinary thing a parent did; howItsDone 'often chanted' softened to 'may be chanted' (claims rule).
Audit: 'says nothing at all' changed to 'at first says nothing', since in the Jataka he does speak (harshly, in many tellings) before he tells her of the gift.
